ED-282-12 [UI][FOUNDATION][COMPOSER] A leaving chip fades where it stands while its place closes (UI-COMPOSER-007; OD-0076).
FOUND (probe): removing the middle quote of three, ForEach's placement of the survivors (`Move(at, i)` by absolute index) put the leaving row behind the row that stayed, so the chip after it jumped left at once and the leaving chip faded at the END of the row, full width, and was dropped from layout when its fade was over (the record's "removal animates on Chrome.panelSlide"; ED-282-3's known limit). SwiftUI takes a leaving view out of the layout at once, draws it fading in place and moves the others under the transaction. DECISION: (1) ForEach places each surviving row straight after the one before it and after any leaving rows that stood there, so a leaving row keeps its place (ForEachLeavingRowTests). (2) Each chip stands in a ChipSlot (the chip, and the 6 point gap after it as the slot's own margin; the row has no spacing and a minus 6 end margin, so chips stand exactly 6 apart). A chip that leaves closes its slot, width and gap, along Chrome.panelSlide while the foundation's fade runs on the chip, which keeps its width and its left edge; the chips after it follow the closing slot under the spring and nothing is left to jump when the fade is over. The glide of the survivors is therefore the layout's, and runs under reduce motion as well (panelSlide's 0.18 s ease-out). Evidence: Removing_the_middle_quote_fades_it_where_it_stands_while_the_chip_after_it_follows_under_the_spring_and_nothing_jumps_at_the_end; mutations chipslot-gap, chipslot-fold, chipslot-minwidth, foreach-leaving-skip killed. The B3 chip-row test's `Spacing == 6` became the slot's 6 point end margin (the gap between two chips is measured in The_command_chip_names_...).

## ED-283

[WIN][KEYBOARD] How ED-270 (the zoom chords are key equivalents of the character typed) is built. ENGINEERING DECISIONS, none a deviation; all inside ED-270's ruling.
1. Which items. The four literal-character items of AppCommands.swift:53-62 (Zoom In "+", Zoom Out "-", Actual Size "0", the hidden Zoom In "=") are marked `MatchesTypedCharacter` (Port/MenuKeyEquivalents.cs, AppCommands.cs). Every other item keeps ED-099's US-position reading, including the nine "Thread n" items, whose literals ED-270 does not name.
2. How a key is read. `MenuKeyEquivalents.Typed` gives the key equivalent of the character the key types on the active layout: Port/KeyboardLayoutText.cs maps the key's Set-1 scan code (ED-099's table) to the active layout's virtual key (MapVirtualKeyExW, MAPVK_VSC_TO_VK_EX) and translates it with ToUnicodeEx under a keyboard state holding Shift only, with flag 4 so the real keyboard state and any pending dead key are untouched; a dead key, an extended key and a control character read as no character. Avalonia's own `KeyEventArgs.KeySymbol` is not used: Avalonia.Win32 fills it with ToUnicodeEx under the modifiers actually held (KeyInterop.GetKeySymbol), which for a Ctrl chord is a control character or nothing, and with Alt (WM_SYSKEYDOWN) from the virtual key alone.
3. Shift. Shift is dropped from the chord only when it is part of typing the character, that is when the key types a different character without Shift (US "=" with Shift types "+"; the French "0" key with Shift types "0"). Shift with the US "0" key types ")" and with the "-" key "_", which no item holds, so those chords stay Ctrl+Shift and reach nothing. ED-230's reading (Shift with the US "=" key is "+") is the US-layout case of this rule.
4. Keypad. The numeric keypad's + and - type those characters on every layout, with or without Shift, so they are read as "+" and "-" without the layout (ED-230 had only "+"; ED-270 names "the keypad plus and minus"). The keypad's 0 is not read as "0": ED-270 names "Ctrl+0", and reading keypad digits as characters would change which commands Ctrl+keypad-digit reaches (ED-230's reason for leaving them out).
5. Order. One pass in body order, as a menu takes the first enabled item holding the chord: an ordinary item compares the chord by position, a literal-character item compares the chord by the character typed, so a user shortcut recorded on Ctrl+Shift+= (position) that sits before Zoom In in the body still wins (ED-230's rule, now a consequence of the order), and in a window without the thread-number monitor (Settings, the tour window, a bare window) the French "-" key, which sits at the US "6" position, reaches Zoom Out before "Thread 6". The main window is different: it is a ThreadWindow, whose digit monitor takes Ctrl with the number row by key position before the menu sees the event (SOURCE FACT, ThreadWindow.swift:11-23, `event.keyCode` 22 is Thread 6), so there the same French chord selects Thread 6 and does not zoom out. CONSEQUENCE of ED-270 (ENGINEERING DECISION, not a deviation): on a French layout the Thread 6 chord cannot be reached from the Settings or tour windows, where Zoom Out takes it; the earlier wording of this item (Zoom Out before Thread 6 "in every window") was wrong for the main window. The character is read only when a literal-character item is reached.
6. Tests. The headless tests' process-wide layout is ANSI US, installed by a module initializer (Fixtures/KeyboardLayouts.cs), so no test reads the PC's layout; a test overrides `KeyboardLayoutText.Current` for its own flow with a table (US, German, French). AppCommandsZoomTests presses the keys through the production dispatch on each (a bare window, and the French chord by window: the main ThreadWindow selects Thread 6, Settings zooms out).
7. The production reader is tested on real layouts, not only on tables. `WindowsKeyboardLayoutText` takes the layout it reads from a `Func<IntPtr>` (the default is `GetKeyboardLayout(0)`, the active layout of the calling thread, which is all the app uses), so a test can bind it to a named layout. Fixtures/WindowsLayoutReaders.cs (an `IDisposable` fixture, one per test) loads the US (00000409), German (00000407) and French (0000040C) layouts into the test process with `LoadKeyboardLayoutW` and KLF_NOTELLSHELL, never KLF_ACTIVATE, so the PC's active layout and the persisted input settings (the user's language list) are untouched and no test depends on them. A loaded layout does join the session's layout list (`GetKeyboardLayoutList`), which the earlier wording of this item overlooked (review of 2026-10-04: after a run the list held French and German until sign-out). Dispose therefore calls `UnloadKeyboardLayout` on every handle the fixture loaded that was not already in `GetKeyboardLayoutList` when the first live fixture started (a layout the list already held, such as the PC's own, is never unloaded; overlapping fixtures unload only when the last is disposed), and fails loudly if Windows will not unload one. AppCommandsZoomTests.The_layout_fixture_leaves_the_sessions_layout_list_and_the_active_layout_as_it_found_them asserts that the list and the active layout are the same before and after, and that the layouts were in the list while the fixture lived. Three kinds of test use it: the tables of Fixtures/KeyboardLayouts.cs are compared with the reader for every key they name, plain and with Shift (so the tables are an honest stand-in, and a reader that ignores Shift or reads a fixed US table fails); the zoom records' test presses Ctrl+Shift+=, Ctrl+=, Ctrl+Shift+0 and the rest through the production main and Settings windows over the reader (a reader that ignores Shift fails it); and the French number-row chord is pressed in both windows. The mutant "the reader ignores Shift", which every table-layout test let live (adversarial review of 2026-10-04), is killed by these tests and by REVIEW_the_Windows_layout_reader_applies_Shift.
8. Closures of the second Blitz review round (2026-10-04, unit appcommands), recorded here as ENGINEERING DECISIONS and test-hygiene facts, none a deviation.
   a. French AZERTY by window (item 5): corrected in item 5 and in the French bare-window test's comment (it names the Settings, tour and bare windows, not the main window); the production main window is asserted by AppCommandsZoomTests.On_a_French_keyboard_Ctrl_with_the_key_that_types_a_minus_selects_Thread_6_in_the_main_window_and_zooms_out_in_the_Settings_window (a ThreadWindow selects Thread 6, Settings zooms out).
   b. Layout list (item 7): the fixture unloads what it loaded; the test above pins it.
   c. The production reader on the keys the zoom chords sit on, with the characters written out and not read from a table: AppCommandsZoomTests.The_Windows_reader_types_the_characters_Windows_gives_the_Equal_Minus_Digit0_BracketRight_and_Slash_keys_on_the_German_and_French_layouts_plain_and_with_Shift reads Equal, Minus, Digit0, BracketRight and Slash plain and with Shift on the loaded US, German and French layouts (German "=" position: a dead accent, no character; French "]" position "$" and "£", "/" position "!" and "§"). A reader over a fixed US table fails every German and French row.
   d. Traceability: AppCommandsFinishTests.The_palette_holds_only_the_source_actions_... (the no-palette-row clause) and ...Ctrl_0_pressed_in_the_focused_Settings_window_... are Rule R-TEST-4 partials with a comment naming the clause they prove. Every record they named keeps a full proof (a Req trait) in another test: PR-WIN-092, PR-WIN-224, UI-WIN-007, PR-WIN-101, PR-WIN-113, PR-WIN-223, UI-WIN-015, UI-WIN-025 and UI-WIN-077 in AppCommandsTests and AppCommandsFinishTests, PR-WIN-222, PR-WIN-224 and UI-WIN-074 also in AppCommandsZoomTests.Read_by_Windows_...; no record lost its proof.

## ED-284

[WIN][SETTINGS][THEME][TEST] Window management (WindowManager.swift; the blitz unit blitz-windowmanager; the lead numbers it at merge). Six decisions, each a necessary internal choice. (1) THE FRAME THAT IS CENTRED AND CLAMPED IS THE VISIBLE WINDOW (WindowManager.swift:43, :46-54, :68, :82). SOURCE FACT: an NSWindow made with .fullSizeContentView has no title bar above its content, so its frame is the content rect the source states (1320 x 860, 780 x 580; :93-96), and window.center() and the clamp into visibleFrame work on that frame. MEASURED on real HWNDs of Avalonia 12.1.2 (WindowManagerNativeTests): a factory window (WindowDecorations.Full with the client area extended under the title bar, ED-063) has an HWND 16 px wider and 8 px taller than its client area (8 px of invisible resize border, SM_CXSIZEFRAME + SM_CXPADDEDBORDER at the window's DPI, on the left, the right and the bottom, none above), also for the fixed Settings window; DWM's visible bounds lie one pixel outside the client area on the left, right and bottom. Before the window has been shown Avalonia reports the standard overlapped frame instead (the client size plus 16 x 39 at 100 %, a caption on top), so the first centring (main window, Settings first open) put the visible window 11 to 15 px too high (measured: 13 px for the main window at 1920 x 1080; Settings 15 px). DECISION: WindowInvisibleBorder (Port) states the strip from the system metrics at the DPI of the monitor the window is about to be on (zero for a window without an HWND, so headless runs are unchanged); WindowCentering.Center centres the visible window, with one third of the free height above it, and places the HWND by it; the clamp keeps the visible window, not the HWND, inside the working area (the strip may lie outside it); the Settings centring over a visible main window adds the strip to its frame and extends the clamp rectangle by it. EXCEPTION, a MAXIMISED main window (review of 2026-10-04): Windows places a maximised HWND with its resize border outside the monitor on all four sides, and Avalonia 12.1.2's WM_NCCALCSIZE maximise branch (decompiled Avalonia.Win32.WindowImpl) insets the client by it on all four sides, so the strip also lies above the client and the HWND centre is the visible centre (a normal window's visible centre lies strip / 2 above its HWND centre). The Settings HWND is centred on the main window's visible centre moved down by strip / 2 (the Settings frame's own bottom strip); for a normal main window that is the HWND centre as before (WindowManagerReviewTests: a 1920 x 1040 working area, a main HWND at (-8, -8) of 1936 x 1056, the Settings HWND at (562, 230), its visible window centred on (960, 520)). Not observed on a real maximised HWND here; the strip above is taken from the decompiled source. The one pixel of DWM's own border is inside the +-1 pixel the native tests allow. (2) AppKit's setFrame(_, display: false) (:54) has no Windows analogue. The origin is computed first and the window is shown after it (cloaked for the Rise open, OD-0074, so no frame at an old position is ever displayed); an already visible window is moved at once. Move-before-Show is the only observable part and is asserted (WindowManagerSettingsPresentationTests.Cached_show_centers_before_the_platform_show_request). The clause is recorded NOT_APPLICABLE for PR-SETTINGS-002 and PR-WIN-011. (3) PR-WIN-008: "backing: .buffered" is NOT_APPLICABLE (an Avalonia window is drawn through DWM's composition buffer; nothing to choose), tabbingMode is NOT_APPLICABLE (as the record says), defer: false is the HWND existing before the first Show (asserted natively). animationBehavior = .documentWindow maps to the system's window animation (the record's windows_path): DWMWA_TRANSITIONS_FORCEDISABLED cannot be read back from DWM (E_INVALIDARG), so it is proved on real pixels: a window hidden over a plain backdrop fades through intermediate frames, a control window with the transitions forced off is cut, and the factory's Settings and main windows fade (WindowManagerNativeChromeTests). The open animation of the Settings and the main window is replaced by owner decisions (OD-0074 Rise, OD-0018 hand-over) and the main window's close is a quit (OD-0008 C1); only the hide the system animates is claimed. (4) PR-THEME-039: Application.RequestedThemeVariant is what NSApp.appearance maps to, and Avalonia sets each window's DWMWA_USE_IMMERSIVE_DARK_MODE from the variant it ends up with: read back from both real factory HWNDs for Dark, Light, Dracula and System (System follows AppsUseLightTheme). The Win32 context menus keep the Windows menu theme (OD-0042), so the record's "native menus out of step" is superseded for them by the owner's ruling. (5) RECORD != SWIFT, Swift wins: the Settings window is an independent NSWindow (:80-84, :57-60); the records' "owned top-level window" and "child window" are not in the source, so the port sets no Owner (asserted: WindowManagerSettingsPresentationTests.Settings_and_main_windows_have_no_owner_relationship). PR-WIN-009's literal fallback "Marrow" is not in the source either (Text.swift:4 falls back to "Droppy Code", kept in Core); the shipped assembly always carries "Marrow" (AssemblyInfo.cs, OD-0002), proved by reading it. (6) The corner wedge of OD-0075 is proved on real pixels for the Settings window: the four corners outside the 26 pt shape read the window's scrim over what the system shows there, in both themes, with the wedge hidden as the control (GlassWindowNativeTests). Fail-first, observed: with the pre-show frame the two native placement tests failed (the main window 13 px, the Settings first open 15 px high) and pass with the fix; the fade test carries its own controls (a window with transitions off is cut, one with them on fades) and the wedge test its own (the wedge layer hidden). The reviewer mutates the rest. Blitz review closures (2026-10-04): (1) the maximised main window (a product defect: Settings 4 px above the centre of a maximised main window at 100 %) is closed by the exception in decision (1) and by WindowManager.CenterOverMainWindow counting the main HWND's top strip when its WindowState is Maximized; WindowManagerReviewTests.REVIEW_Settings_is_centred_over_a_maximised_main_window_whose_HWND_strip_lies_on_all_four_sides passes unchanged in its expectation (562, 230) (it sets WindowState = Maximized, the state its name claims); the strip above a maximised HWND comes from the decompiled WM_NCCALCSIZE branch and was not observed on a real maximised HWND, and a FullScreen main window has no case (no evidence for its strip; behaviour unchanged). (2) the strip arithmetic is pinned by Req-traited headless tests that stand in a strip of 12 px (the older R-TEST-4 tests use 8 px): WindowManagerCenteringTests.The_HWND_is_placed_one_invisible_strip_left_of_the_centred_visible_window_and_at_its_top (PR-WIN-006: the border term of WindowCentering.Center on the left and no term above), A_visible_main_window_larger_than_the_work_area_keeps_its_left_edge_on_it_and_the_strip_outside_it (PR-WIN-006: the clamp term of Center), The_Settings_HWND_without_a_main_window_is_placed_one_invisible_strip_left_of_the_centred_visible_window (PR-WIN-010, PR-SETTINGS-002); WindowManagerSettingsScreenTests.The_Settings_frame_carries_its_own_invisible_strip_when_centred_on_the_visible_main_window (the strip in the Settings frame) and The_clamp_extension_by_a_strip_of_12_px_lets_the_HWND_lie_outside_the_working_area_by_the_strip (the clamp rectangle's left, right and bottom extension; PR-SETTINGS-002, PR-WIN-011). Each is headless arithmetic with the strip stood in; that a real HWND has the strip stays WindowManagerNativeTests. The checker mutates them.

## ED-297

[UI][SHAPES][GLASS][OD-0102] How the band is built (unit blitz-cornerband, 2026-10-04; the lead numbers this heading at merge). OD-0102 and ED-275 (2) say what is drawn; these items say how, and are ENGINEERING DECISIONS unless they say SOURCE FACT.

(1) THE RULE, per corner (SwiftShapes.ResolveCorners, one function behind Outline, the cached geometry, the Border clip, SwiftShapeBorder and HasContinuousCorner). Radius 0 is square. `.circular` is the circular arc held to half the shorter side. `.continuous`: where the corner's run-in and its neighbour's fit along each side they share (`E * a + E * b <= side`, E = 1.528665, as before) it is Apple's corner at the stated radius; else, when the stated radius is under half the shorter side (`r < min(w, h) / 2`), it is Apple's corner at `min(r, LargestRadius(size))`, for a uniform radius exactly `min(w, h) / (2 E)`, so the two run-ins of a short side meet at its middle; else (r at least half: a capsule) the circular arc held to half. For an UnevenRoundedRectangle each band corner takes `min(its radius, LargestRadius)` and is then re-checked against its neighbours' drawn radii; a corner whose neighbour still does not fit stays the circular arc. The uneven rule is mine (OD-0102 states the uniform case; Apple's clamping of an uneven shape is not documented, ED-275 (7)); no site in the app is known to draw an uneven shape in the band, and the test pins the rule so it is not silent.

(2) THE EXEMPTION, SOURCE FACT for the measurement (ED-275 (2): the composer, r 22 on 46 pt, circle 0.156 px rms, iOS 7 shape_2 0.212, clamped corner 1.148) and OD-0102's own EXCEPT clause. `SwiftShapes.CircularInBandProperty` (an attached bool, set with `.CircularInBand()`; `GlassShape.RoundedRectangle(r, style, circularInBand: true)` for the glass) marks a `.continuous` shape that a reference frame measures circular where Apple's corner does not fit; such a shape keeps the circular arc in the band and is Apple's corner as soon as the full corner fits. Set on exactly the composer pill: ComposerSurface (ComposerView.swift:1298) and the working-dots slot's clip (:671, the same pill's overlay, r 22). ENGINEERING DECISION inside that: the exemption is the ELEMENT's, so a composer between 46 pt and 67.3 pt (two lines, growing) also stays circular; no recording shows a multi-line composer, so no frame measures it and no frame contradicts it, and a composer that switched from the measured circle to the clamped corner while it grew would jump. If the owner wants the exemption only at the measured height, it is one condition in ResolveCorners.

(3) THE STROKE AND THE CLIP are on the same curve. A plain Border is cut by `ContinuousClip` to `ClipOutline` built from the same resolver (it still takes no clip while the corners are circular); a SwiftShapeBorder fills, clips and hit-tests the outline and strokes SwiftUI's `strokeBorder`: the inset path is built from the DRAWN radii (`ShapeOutline.DrawnRadius(i)`, new: 0 square, the arc radius, or Apple's curve radius) less half the width, so in the band the stroke's outer edge is the shape at the largest radius that fits (SwiftShapesBandTests: the ring's 45 degree crossing at `0.2915 L` per axis, not at the circle of r 18). The inset path is re-resolved on the smaller rectangle, so its radius is `(h - width) / (2 E)`, 0.35 of a half-width from concentric: below what a pixel shows, and the same approximation the full-corner regime already has. The geometry cache key carries the exemption flag.

(4) THE GLASS. The shader's `shapeDistance` takes the band too: for a rounded rectangle with `continuous == 1`, a corner radius above `min(c.x, c.y) / E` and under `min(c.x, c.y)` is replaced by `min(c.x, c.y) / E` before the distance is computed (the factor E is substituted into the shader text from `ContinuousCorner.Extent`); `continuous == 2` is the exemption and keeps the circle. The mirror `ContinuousCorner.Distance(point, half, radius, continuous, circularInBand)` does the same; GlassContinuousCornerTests run the shader on Skia's CPU rasteriser against the mirror (1e-3 px) at the band sizes and the composer, and the mirror's zero level against the path (0.05 px) at 380 x 40, 380 x 48 and 380 x 54 (r 18).

(5) WHAT CHANGED IN TESTS (none weakened; each was a pin of the circular arc in the band, or of a size that is now in it): SwiftShapesContinuousTests (the regime boundary above the limit, the uneven 30 x 40 case, the composer outline, the no-clip case), SwiftShapeBorderTests (the circular-regime pixel test marks the composer), SwiftShapesOracleTests (the composer end is fitted with the exemption), GlassContinuousCornerTests (the circle-distance test marks the composer; the mirror theory gains the band sizes and `continuous == 2`), ContinuousCornerChecks.Drawn (probes the sliver at the drawn radius), TimelineRowsFinFileCardTests and TimelineRowsPrRecordsTests (the 40 pt Edited-files card is Apple's corner), the composer glass-shape equalities in ComposerViewTests and ComposerViewBlitzPillTests, the working-dots clip test. New: SwiftShapesBandTests (path, regimes, exemption, mounted fill, clip, stroke) and four Req tests in ContinuousCornerReproofTests, one per record, each reading the corner off the mounted element (every corner Apple's at height / 3.057, the 12 control points, the clip, the neighbouring capsule or full corner).

(6) CHECKED: the Corner Band page's JS port (E:\Droppy\work\design\decisions-2026-10-04\corner-band\src\cb-geometry.js, optionA) agrees with the C# at 380 x 40, 43, 48 and 54 (r 18): the same radius (13.0833, 14.0646, 15.6999, 17.6625), 12 cubics, no arc, the run-in ending at h / 2, control points within 3.6e-7 of SPEC.md 1.2's vector scaled to that radius (the vector's own rounding), scratch E:\Droppy\work\scratch\cornerband\check_js.js.

(7) NOT DONE, tracked: ED-275 (7)'s raw `CornerRadius` Borders that never call `.RoundedRectangle(...)` stay circular in every regime, band included, until their unit adds the call; the custom renders (RowGlide, TokenActivitySection cells, AttachmentFlightPlatform, ComposerLightRenderer's mask) are unchanged. AMENDED by (10) (CB-0 fix, 2026-10-04): the Borders that can sit in the band are routed; the rest are classed.

(8) WHAT A PLAIN BORDER IN THE BAND FILLS (blitz-cornerband review, 2026-10-04; corrects (3)). (3) said the plain Border's fill and its clip are on the same curve. In the band they were not: the Border kept CornerRadius 18, so Avalonia filled the circle of 18, and a clip can only remove fill; Apple's corner at L = `h / (2 E)` lies OUTSIDE that circle near the diagonal (2.06 pt at h 40, 1.66 at 43, 0.98 at 46 and 48, 0.17 at 54), so the screen showed the circle of 18 (option B) or the overlap of the two, not OD-0102's option A (measured: the top-left 8 x 8 differed from a SwiftShapeBorder's path fill by up to 255 of 255). The checks that passed then read the outline data, the clip object and `FillContains` on the clip path, never the pixels. ENGINEERING DECISION: `ContinuousClip`'s tracker keeps the radius the site stated (`SwiftShapes.StatedCornerRadius(border)`; what the clip, `Outline`, the glass and every test of the stated radius read) and sets the Border's own `CornerRadius` (`SetCurrentValue`, so a binding or a style still applies) to `SwiftShapes.DrawnCornerRadius`: for a corner that is Apple's in the band it carries 0 when this tracker's clip is what cuts the Border and the Border has no border ring (the Border fills its pixel-aligned rectangle and the clip, Apple's path, is the only anti-aliased edge, so the corner is the path fill within the clip's own anti-aliasing: 49 of 255 at the worst pixel, two pixels of the bottom run-in, where a circular fill under the clip multiplied two anti-aliased edges and differed by 91); otherwise the radius it is drawn at, L (the circle of L is Apple's curve to 0.0138 L inside and 0.002 L outside, what a ring or a shadow needs, and the Border without our clip). Every other corner (a fit, a capsule, the composer's exemption, a square corner) keeps its stated radius, so the regimes outside the band are exactly as before. The glass reads the stated radius (its shader makes the corner, OD-0102). The shapes the earlier tests read through `Border.CornerRadius` now read `StatedCornerRadius` (ContinuousCornerChecks.Drawn, ContinuousCornerReproofTests): the same expectation, on the stated radius. Tests: SwiftShapesBandTests (the fill-only pixels, a ring, a shadow, the site's own clip, the regimes as the size and the radius change, `DrawnCornerRadius`), ContinuousCornerReproofTests.REVIEW_the_four_band_elements_render_Apples_corner_... (the four mounted elements against the path fill). UNRESOLVED (a rasteriser fact, not a defect of the shape): at 200 x 40 the clip's anti-aliasing differs from a SwiftShapeBorder's path fill by 49 of 255 at the worst pixel (two pixels of the bottom run-in: 128 and 160 against 177 and 192; every other pixel of the corner within 32), headless Skia raster. Measured why (scratch, 2026-10-04): the same Border cut by the EXACT outline (no slack) equals the path fill to within 1 level, and so does the outline drawn as a fill; any slack structure of ClipOutline, even 0.001 pt below the bottom side, gives the 128 and 160 (the top row of the same corner is identical in both, 178 and 226), so the 49 comes from the slack that ED-275 (3) keeps for children drawn beyond a side, not from the corner. SwiftShapesBandTests.REVIEW_a_plain_Border_in_the_band_draws_Apples_corner_... requires under 40 and so fails; the owner's choice is a tolerance of 50 there, or no slack on the straight sides (a child drawn beyond a side is then cut, which ED-275 (3) rejected). The four band records are proven on their mounted elements at a tolerance of 60 (the Edited-files card, h 40, among them). RESOLVED by (9) (CB-0 fix, 2026-10-04): the 49 is Skia's anti-aliasing of a non-convex path, not the slack's size; a Border that draws nothing beyond a side is cut by the exact outline and measures within 1 level.

(9) THE CLIP'S ANTI-ALIASING AT ANY BOUND SIZE (CB-0 fix, 2026-10-04; resolves (8)'s UNRESOLVED and the re-review's second defect). The re-review attributed the 49 of 255 (UI-CHAT-034's REVIEW test requires under 40) to huge clip bounds (ClipSlack 4096). MEASURED, and the cause is not the size: with SkiaSharp directly (a 220 x 60 raster, a red 200 x 40 rect under `ClipPath(path, antialias)` against `DrawPath(exact outline)`, scratch E:\Droppy\work\scratch\cornerband\skia_scratch.txt and aa_scratch.txt) the exact outline is 0 levels off the path fill (it is CONVEX: `SKPath.IsConvex`), while every NON-convex path is 38 to 49 off at its worst pixel (49 at (21, 49) for all but the last two): the slack clip at a slack of 0.001, 1, 4, 64, 4096 or 1000 (no difference), the exact outline with a notch of 0.5 pt in the middle of the top side, the slack path with its 32-segment flattened cubics (48), with EvenOdd, with its bottom walls slanted or given a horizontal run, a `GeometryGroup` or `CombinedGeometry` union of the exact outline and a rectangle below the bottom side, and the four corner wedges subtracted one by one as difference clips (38). Skia anti-aliases a convex path with its exact walker and any other with a coarser one, so the clip is wrong by tens of levels along every Apple-regime curve (not only the two worst pixels: the right edge column at 200 x 40 is 8 to 23 levels light along its whole curve) and, at other sizes, far more: 102 at 380 x 46, 64 at 60 x 40, 24 at 380 x 54 and 1500 x 54, 28 at 300 x 30 (r 12). No amount of building the path smaller helps, and a convex path cannot reach beyond a straight side, so the slack that ED-275 (3) keeps for children drawn beyond a side cannot be both. ENGINEERING DECISION: `ContinuousClip` cuts a Border by the EXACT outline (`SwiftShapes.ClipGeometry(rect, radii, circularInBand, exact: true)`, `ClipOutline(..., exact: true)`: `Build` with slack 0, the cached geometry's key carries the flag) when the Border can draw nothing beyond a side and every rounded corner is Apple's: it has no Child, or it is clipped to its bounds (`ClipToBounds`), and `SwiftShapes.ExactClipFits(size, radii, circularInBand)` (no corner resolves to an arc: an arc is the Border's own corner, and the same arc as a clip would be anti-aliased twice, (8)). Otherwise the slack clip of (3) is unchanged and keeps its measured 49 (the four band records' mounted elements have children: their tolerance of 60 stands). The tracker also follows `Decorator.ChildProperty`, so a Border that gains or loses its child changes clip. Measured after, a childless plain Border against a SwiftShapeBorder of the same shape, worst pixel of 255: 0 at 60 x 40, 1 at 200 x 40 (the REVIEW test; 49 before), 380 x 46, 380 x 54, 1500 x 40 and 1500 x 54 (r 18), 8 at 300 x 30 (r 12). NOT FIXED, stated: a Border WITH a child that is not clipped to its bounds still takes the slack clip and keeps the numbers above (64, 49, 102, 24, 49, 24 and 28 for the same sizes in order; the mounted band elements are within the tolerance of 60 their tests carry); only a clip that is both convex and reaches beyond a side would fix it and none exists, so the owner's choice there is the one (8) named: no slack (a child drawn beyond a side is cut, which ED-275 (3) rejected) or this error. Consequence taken, ENGINEERING DECISION: the exact outline's straight sides lie on the Border's own edge, so at a position that is not pixel aligned an edge pixel's coverage is multiplied by the fill's (0.5 becomes 0.25); layout rounding keeps a settled Border aligned and the slack clip never had this, so a Border moved by a fractional transform shows its straight edge slightly thinner while it moves. Tests: SwiftShapesBandTests (the REVIEW test at its original tolerance of 40; `A_childless_plain_Border_in_the_band_matches_the_path_fill_at_every_bound_size...` for the sizes above; `A_Border_that_cannot_draw_beyond_its_sides_is_cut_by_the_exact_outline_and_one_that_can_keeps_the_slack`; `A_corner_that_is_an_arc_keeps_the_slack_clip...`), the clip identities in SwiftShapesContinuousTests and ContinuousCornerChecks.ExpectedClip, and UI-CHAT-034's Req test restored (it had been withdrawn for the 49).

## ED-285

[UI][CHAT] The TimelineRows closing pass of 2026-10-04 (unit blitz-timelinerows-ab, OD-0098: where no reference frame exists the pinned Swift source is the proof). (1) THE CHECKLIST'S ANIMATION. SOURCE FACT: TodoListRow carries `.animation(.snappy(duration: 0.2), value: steps)` (TimelineRows.swift:2372), so a change of the steps is interpolated by SwiftUI: the foreground styles of a step's glyph (:2355) and text (:2357) move from their old colour to the new one, and a step that arrives or goes is inserted or removed under the default transition of a view in a stack, an opacity. The port opened the same transaction but set every colour and added every row directly, so nothing moved. DECIDED (ENGINEERING DECISION, OD-0076: every change transitioned): each step keeps one AnimatedColor for its glyph and one for its text, set inside the transaction (a step arriving is set at once, not tweened from nothing), and rows arrive and leave through SwiftTransition (opacity). The glyph itself (circle, circle.dotted.circle, checkmark.circle.fill) was replaced at once and the card's own size was not animated: SUPERSEDED by (12), which crossfades the glyph and the count and eases the card. (2) THE TURN-END DURATIONS. The strings PR-CHAT-116 expects for 0, a negative interval, a half second, 60, 3599, 3600 and 3725 seconds are the narrow-width Duration.UnitsFormatStyle output as ED-197 (oracle O-65) reads it from swift-foundation 6.2's `Duration+UnitsFormatStyle.swift`, the framework's documented behaviour the code relies on (Components.swift:37-40); under OD-0098 they close the record, labelled ENGINEERING DECISION, and stay tied to O-65 for a later macOS run. (3) HOW A TRANSLUCENT ICON IS READ IN A RENDER. Lucide icons are drawn one element at a time, so where two strokes of a translucent icon overlap (a corner) the pixel is composited twice and reads up to about 1.5 of the single colour; the render checks of the tool, chevron and card glyphs (BlitzAbRender.InkIsColour) allow that factor and no more. A Mac SF symbol is one shape and has no such overlap: a visual difference of ED-182's named compromises, not claimed here. ENGINEERING DECISION.

(8) HOW INK IS COMPARED. A line or a symbol drawn in a source ink is compared with the same line or symbol drawn alone in that ink in a window of its own, by the summed distance of its pixels from the backdrop (its mass), not by its peak: a thin stroke at 10 points never reaches the colour whole and a mark half a pixel off its grid changes its peak, not its mass. SwiftColor.MixPerceptual (Marrow.UI) interpolates in Oklab (Ottosson's published matrices, from the linear light of the sRGB components, the opacity linearly, clamped and encoded back) and EffortPalette.Title and EffortPairBrand.TitleColors use it; SwiftColor.Mix stays the component-wise interpolation. [VOICE][BUILD][TEST] Voice typing phase V0, unit VT-0 (the pins; the lead numbers these at merge). ENGINEERING DECISIONS inside OD-0091, OD-0092, OD-0097 and the OD-0099 picks (Q-V-5, Q-V-9 C); none is a deviation from the owner's rulings.
1. The pins. Directory.Packages.props pins Whisper.net, Whisper.net.Runtime and Whisper.net.Runtime.Vulkan 1.9.1 and NAudio.Wasapi 3.1.0 (voice SPEC V-3.1; the lead delegated this one edit to VT-0, the file's header still holds for everything else); Marrow.Services.csproj references them without versions. All rights reserved." (dotnet/extensions LICENSE), System.Numerics.Tensors ".NET Foundation and Contributors" (LICENSE.TXT inside the package), NAudio "Mark Heath", Metal as Whisper.net "sandrohanea"). No CUDA, no-AVX, OpenAI or ONNX package is referenced (V-3.1 "Not taken", Q-V-9 C).
2. Trimming the natives (V-3.2). The runtime packages' build targets add the natives of EVERY platform to the copy list (win-arm64, win-x86, Linux Vulkan: 126,744,840 bytes for a win-x64 app). Marrow.Services.csproj gets the target MarrowTrimWhisperNatives, which removes every runtimes/ item except runtimes/win-x64/ (CPU) and runtimes/vulkan/win-x64/ before AssignTargetPaths, so the extra files reach neither the Services output, nor an app or test project that references it, nor the self-contained publish (checked with `dotnet publish src/Marrow.App -c Release -r win-x64 --self-contained`: nine native files, no others; round 2 saved the publish's file list, names, sizes and sha256, as porting/probes/vt-0-publish/publish-listing.txt and VoicePinsTests holds the nine files and the two assets to it). Whisper.net's loader finds exactly this layout (runtimes\vulkan\win-x64 for Vulkan, runtimes\win-x64 for the CPU).

V-3.2's "CPU + Vulkan natives under 50 MB unpacked" was a RESEARCH ESTIMATE; measured 61,957,120 bytes unpacked (ggml-vulkan-whisper.dll alone is 58,013,696), about 18.9 MB deflated. The record says withinBudget false and the report names it in its notDone list (round 2: round 1's report did not, so the lead could read the row's "budget under 50 MB" as met; it is NOT met: 61,957,120 bytes against 50,000,000, over by 11,957,120, and the lead or the owner decides whether the estimate stands or the Vulkan backend moves to a download); nothing is dropped to hit a number the spec called an estimate.

SOURCE FACT from the PE import tables of the shipped files: the whisper natives import MSVCP140, VCRUNTIME140, VCRUNTIME140_1 and VCOMP140; the app itself (coreclr, hostpolicy, Marrow.App.exe, libSkiaSharp, libHarfBuzzSharp, av_libglesv2) imports only the Universal CRT or nothing, and the publish carries none of the four DLLs (round 2: backed by the saved publish listing porting/probes/vt-0-publish/publish-listing.txt, 251 files, and VoicePinsTests fails if vcRuntime.carriedByPublish disagrees with it). BUILD-PLAN section 4 item F confirms it on a clean PC.

Although there is something written on the back of the document, it is not a treasure map.") at dataset commit 70bb2e84 (CC BY 4.0 per the dataset card), 10.02 s, 16 kHz mono 16-bit, which is BENCH's own timing clip en_10s_1: byte-identical (sha256 5c3db892...), reproduced from the archive member with BENCH's recipe (scripts/prep_audio.py: decode with ffmpeg to 16 kHz mono 16-bit, scale by one gain 3000 / rms = 1.062187, capped so the peak stays at or under 30000; the decoded RMS was 2824.36 and the peak 23950, so the cap did not apply). REPRODUCED (porting/probes/vt-0-cuda-loader: probe source, run script, the saved output of seventeen runs and the pack's saved import tables, 2026-10-04; VoicePinsTests and VoicePinsReview3Tests hold the record to those files; round 3 re-ran the whole probe with the real pack): Whisper.net 1.9.1 loads the CPU runtime (case 1), the Vulkan runtime (case 4) and the REAL Whisper.net.Runtime.Cuda12.Windows 1.9.1 runtime (case 9: the pack's five files and the NVIDIA 12.4 cudart, cublas and cublasLt in <root>\runtimes\cuda12\win-x64, order [Cuda12]: LoadedLibrary=Cuda12, the Silero VAD finds the same three segments) from a downloaded folder. ## ED-288

[FIRSTRUN][COMPOSER][TEST] GR-1, the first-run preparation service (BUILD-PLAN 2.2; OD-0096 and the OD-0098 amendments "Look I, Words W1, Download D3"; builds on ED-252). Each reading is an ENGINEERING DECISION where the picked page and the spec are silent. (1) THE REGISTRY. GpuWarmup holds a registry of entries, GpuProgram: a program that draws on the render thread (GpuProgram.Draw: handed the window's GPU context and scaling) or a step of other work (GpuProgram.Work: awaited on the UI thread). Each names its first-run step with a FirstRunStep (id, W1's name, order; the ids are gr_lib.py:20-23's: gpu, knob, lights, liquid, strike, hw; the orders 10 to 60). The registry keeps entries in step order, then registration order; Register refuses a name already registered, a step id given another name or order, and an order another step has (a step's entries stay together); disposing the registration removes it. A pass of a warm-up takes the registry as it is when the pass begins. The jewel's four programs (noise, fluid, orb, page: step Knob), the composer light's three (light-rotate, light-moving, light-aura: Border beam's Large with its blob bake, its Line and pulses' moving shader, the Uiverse light, each through ComposerLightRenderer.Draw into a 16 px surface), the slider liquid's (liquid: LiquidTrack.Draw of Grok's tube, oil and a rising bubble, into a GpuWarmup.WarmTarget) and the strike's (strike: the same with the lightning 35 ms into strike 1, which lights the glass pass) are registered in GpuWarmup.cs; the voice orbs (VT-8), a new strike (ST-3) and the voice hardware check (VT-15) register from their own files and join without GpuWarmup.cs being edited. GpuWarmup.Programs and Steps count the programs that draw; a work step is no program and makes no cache entry, so IsWarm and the marker count entries over the programs that draw only. (2) HOW AN UNREGISTERED STEP SHOWS: IT DOES NOT. FirstRunPreparation.Plan lists the Graphics card (its own read of the adapter and driver, GpuWarmup.PrepareGraphicsAsync) and every step that has an entry registered under it; a W1 step with nothing registered has no row and no tick (no work is done for it, and a tick would say it was). Voice hardware is therefore absent from the plan until VT-15 registers its work step; then it joins as the sixth, in W1's order. A step registered later with a FirstRunStep of its own joins by its order. A program naming the step id gpu takes the Graphics card step's name and order. (3) WHAT PROGRESS IS. A step's parts are the Graphics card's read (one) and each entry registered under the step; its fraction is the parts done over its parts (FirstRunProgress.Fraction). The run reports an event when work has BEGUN (a step is Running from when the step before it completed, the first from the start of the run) and when a part has COMPLETED (a program drawn or a work step awaited: GpuWarmup's own reports, one per entry); nothing else. The service's clock (TimeProvider) is read only to stamp an event with the run's elapsed time; no event waits for it and none is caused by it (tested with a manual clock advanced by five hours: not one event more). (4) A run that completes sets Done on a step the warm-up reported nothing for (the CPU renderer has no program to compile ahead: GpuWarmup returns, its work steps still run): the work of such a step is complete. A run that fails or is cancelled ticks nothing it did not do. (5) THE RUN. FirstRunPreparation.RunAsync(window, screen): no screen, NotShown, nothing runs and nothing is read (startup unchanged); IsPrepared (GpuWarmup.IsWarm: the marker naming the build, the adapter and the driver, an entry for each program that draws), Skipped, the screen never told; otherwise Begin(plan), the events, then EndAsync(outcome) awaited, with Prepared, or Failed (the exception's message: a step not drawn within 10 s, a window closed, a program that threw) or Cancelled. A failed run leaves the marker unwritten (GpuWarmup writes it only when a pass completes with an entry for every program and every registered step of other work has been done: (14)), so the next launch prepares again. One run at a time through FirstRunStartup: asking while one runs gives that run. (6) WORK STEPS run in a first-run warm-up (WarmAsync) only, in their step's place, once per run (a pass started again by a new GPU context does not repeat them), and also on the CPU renderer (the voice hardware check needs no GPU); the idle fallback (the model chip's WhenIdle) never runs one. (7) A drawn program that throws on the render thread faults the warm-up with its exception (the run fails; it never completes as if prepared) and leaves the render thread running; before, no program could throw. (8) UNVERIFIED ON A GPU until the supervised native session (the tests run the programs on the CPU renderer with GpuWarmup.PretendGpu, on the UI thread of the headless renderer): that the light, liquid and strike programs make the programs the owner's first visible draw finds (the targets are offscreen RGBA surfaces, as the knob's are, not the window's framebuffer, so a framebuffer-specific variant of a program could still compile at first use); that WarmTarget's reflection on Avalonia.Skia's DrawingContextImpl and Avalonia.Base's PlatformDrawingContext (see (11)) works with a real GPU context; that each new program makes at least one entry in ANGLE's blob cache (the marker needs one entry per program that draws: if one makes none the marker is never written and the sheet would show on every launch; a per-program entry count is the way to tune it); and that the strike's burst rings and the strike's other paints are covered by the one strike frame. (9) The idle fallback warms every registered program that draws, one a frame at idle as before (the 54 EffortSliderJewelWarmup tests pin that a run draws every registered program), so the composer's model chip now warms nine programs. (10) NOT WIRED TO STARTUP: FirstRunStartup.RunAsync is the entry and FirstRunStartup.Screen the seam; GR-2 sets the screen from its startup hook (DroppyCodeApp.cs / AppDelegate.cs, GR-2's files). Until then nothing calls it and startup is unchanged (porting/STATE.md). Everything that registers must have registered before IsPrepared or Plan is first asked. (11) REVIEW ROUND 1 (the liquid and strike target). A RenderTargetBitmap is NOT GPU-backed: in Avalonia 12.1.2 it is always a CPU raster (Avalonia.Skia decompiled: PlatformRenderInterface.CreateRenderTargetBitmap returns RenderTargetBitmapImpl, a WriteableBitmapImpl drawn through a FramebufferRenderTarget, with no GRContext), and LiquidTrack makes its surfaces on lease.GrContext only when it has one, so the first version compiled nothing and reported the two steps done: this replaces the claim in (1) and (8) and the code comment that said otherwise. The liquid and the strike now draw through GpuWarmup.WarmTarget: a surface the window's GPU context makes (SKSurface.Create(gpu, ...); a context that makes none fails the target, never a draw on the CPU reported as the GPU's) and a DrawingContext over a drawing-context impl that names that context (Avalonia.Skia's DrawingContextImpl.CreateInfo Surface, GrContext, Dpi and ScaleDrawingToDpi, wrapped by Avalonia.Base's PlatformDrawingContext as DrawingContextHelper.RenderAsync wraps one), so LiquidTrack.Draw's own custom operation reads the GPU's lease and makes and compiles on it, at the window's scaling. Both types are internal to Avalonia: they are read once by reflection (as GpuWarmup already reads Avalonia's clock), a test pins that the pinned Avalonia has them, and where one is missing the program faults the warm-up (the run fails) instead of drawing elsewhere. On the CPU renderer the programs are not drawn at all (as before), so the idle fallback no longer rasterises two liquid frames at every launch. (12) PROGRESS COUNTS DISTINCT WORK. The run counts each program once; when the warm-up starts a pass again on a new GPU context (ED-252: it reports its programs again), the report of a program already counted takes back the ticks of every program that draws (a step of other work is never taken back, it is done once) and the steps stand as the work done on the context the run ends on: a step already Done shows Running again, a later one Waiting, and each is Done only when its programs have been drawn again (FirstRunProgress already carries Waiting). (13) A WORK STEP THE RUN DID NOT DO IS NEVER TICKED. WarmAsync called while an idle-gated run of the window is going (begun by a new scaling or GPU context; its items leave the work steps out) hurries that run to its end silently and then runs its own pass, which reports every program and step and runs the work steps (the programs are found made, the draws are quick), instead of joining it and reporting nothing for the work steps. FirstRunPreparation's end-of-run tick covers only steps that had draws to compile (the CPU renderer has none); a step with a registered work step that was never reported fails the run (Failed, naming the step) rather than ticking Done. (14) REVIEW ROUND 2: THE MARKER WAITS FOR THE WORK STEPS. The prepared state is the marker (ED-252), and the idle fallback (WhenIdle) never runs a work step yet wrote the marker when its pass of the draws completed, so a first run that failed or was cancelled before its work step (Voice hardware, VT-15) followed by any composer in the session made the next launch Skipped and the hardware check never ran (voice SPEC V-10.5 and V-10.7: it runs again at the next first-run moment). GpuWarmup now records the work steps done in this process (only a first-run warm-up's pass does one) and a pass writes the marker only when every step of other work registered at that moment is among them (none registered: as before, so ED-252 and its tests are unchanged); a work step another unit registers joins the prepared state with no edit to GpuWarmup.cs or FirstRunPreparation.cs. The record is the process's, not the disk's: a first run that did every step writes the marker itself; one that did not leaves it unwritten for any later pass of the session. Disposing a registration forgets its record. (15) REVIEW ROUND 2: A DRAW THAT FAILS INSIDE A TARGET'S OPERATION FAULTS ITS PROGRAM. Avalonia.Base's PlatformDrawingContext.Custom (12.1.2, decompiled) catches what a custom operation's Render throws and only logs it (area Visual, level Error, the operation as source, the exception as the one property), so LiquidTrack.Draw into a WarmTarget returned normally when its operation failed on the render thread (a shader or effect failure, a GPU surface or device fault) and the step was reported done. DrawingContext cannot be subclassed outside Avalonia (its constructor is internal), so the target listens: while any WarmTarget is open an ErrorSink stands over Avalonia.Logging.Logger.Sink (the app's own sink, if any, still hears every event it enabled; this build sets none), keeps the first exception logged by an ICustomDrawOperation under Visual at Error on the thread that opened the target (a thread watches the target it opened last), and WarmTarget.Dispose throws it with its own stack after letting the surface and the context go; the last target to close puts the app's sink back (unless something else replaced it meanwhile). The throw reaches GpuProgram.Draw's contract (ED-288 (7)): the warm-up faults, the step is not reported done and the marker is not written. A target opened on one thread and drawn on another hears nothing (none does: a program draws on the render thread it was handed). The check costs no GPU readback. (16) REVIEW ROUND 2: THE STAND-IN GPU CONTEXT IN TESTS. GpuWarmupReview1Tests' stand-in GRContext (no native object) crashed the test host (0xC0000005) when an assertion on it failed, because xunit formats a failing Assert.Same or Assert.Equal's operands by reading their properties (GRContext.Backend on Handle 0): the run aborted with the later tests' results lost. No assertion is handed the stand-in any more: identity is asserted as a boolean with its own message, so a regression is a named failure. (17) REVIEW ROUND 3: THE CPU RENDERER'S PREPARED STATE SURVIVES THE LAUNCH. On the CPU renderer (Avalonia's Win32 software fallback, used when ANGLE/D3D11 cannot be made: the window's GPU context is null and no cache folder exists) a warm-up pass has no program to compile or keep, returns early and so wrote no marker: IsWarm stayed false, and every launch would have run the first run again (the screen of GR-2 every launch, and once VT-15 registers its work step the voice hardware probe too), against OD-0096 ("again only when the prepared state is invalid ... Later launches skip it") and W1's subtitle ("This happens once."). ENGINEERING DECISION: a pass that ends on the CPU renderer with every registered work step done (the same bar as the GPU marker, (14)) writes a CPU marker, warm-cpu.txt in the cache root (GpuProgramCache.MarkWarmOnCpu: the root is made if it is not there; three lines: this build, "cpu", the adapter and driver the app draws with, DXGI, as the GPU marker names them), and IsWarm is true when that marker names this build and this machine as it is now, or when the GPU marker holds as before. A new build, a driver update, another adapter, or a machine DXGI cannot name (nothing is written for it: not proven) is invalid for it exactly as for the GPU's, and the first run happens again. It is written whole (beside, then moved), not rewritten when it already holds the same, and a completed warm-up on a GPU (MarkWarm) removes its own adapter's record: that adapter is then proven on its GPU ((20) keeps one record for each adapter). The CPU marker does NOT cover a GPU whose blob cache does not install (GpuProgramCache.Folder stays null): that pass draws on the GPU, so it is no CPU pass, and it writes no marker of either kind, because the GPU marker needs the folder's entries; the first run happens on every launch there (unchanged by round 4, and not decided by it: UNRESOLVED until the supervised native session shows whether ANGLE's blob cache installs on the owner's machine). A launch that draws on the GPU after a CPU first run is not skipped by the CPU marker ((18) withdraws the "known and accepted" skip this text first gave). The idle fallback on the CPU renderer writes it too (it had no way to tell a first run from an idle pass, and none is needed: the bar is the work steps). The marker's own adapter and driver comparison (GpuWarmup.IsWarm, third line) is also pinned by a GR-1 test of its own now: a marker written for another adapter, with the folder's key naming this one, is not prepared (the invalidation test alone did not tell it from GpuProgramCache.MadeHere, which compares the same machine through the key). (18) REVIEW ROUND 4: THE CPU MARKER COUNTS ONLY WHILE THE APP DRAWS ON THE CPU RENDERER. The CPU marker names the machine by GpuProgramCache.Machine(), the DXGI adapter and driver, which reads the same whether ANGLE came up or Avalonia fell back to software, and IsWarm checked it first; so a launch that now drew on the GPU (ANGLE up on the same adapter and driver: a transient D3D11 failure at the first run, the GLES library briefly locked, a driver repair that keeps its version string) was Skipped though no program was ever made or kept on that GPU, and with a registered work step (the idle fallback never runs one, so it never writes the GPU marker, (14)) every launch on the GPU stayed Skipped for as long as the build and the driver lasted. ENGINEERING DECISION: IsWarm counts the CPU marker only when GpuWarmup.DrawsOnCpu: Avalonia's Win32 platform bound no graphics platform (IPlatformGraphics: ANGLE/D3D11, else WGL; none is bound when both fail and it draws with the software renderer), and no test pretends a GPU. That is known as soon as the platform is up, before any window, so the same answer serves the startup check, IsPrepared and RunAsync with its window. The locator is not in Avalonia's reference assembly (PrivateApi), so it is read by reflection once, like the clock; where it cannot be read the answer is not-on-the-CPU (the CPU marker then counts for nothing, the GPU marker is the only prepared state, and the first run happens: the safe side), and a test pins that the pinned Avalonia is read and that the headless platform draws on the CPU. A launch that draws on the GPU needs the GPU marker, whatever a CPU marker says. The ED-252 idle fallback is no longer relied on for it: ED (17)'s "known and accepted" skip is withdrawn. Known and not changed: a GPU platform whose blob cache does not install (GpuProgramCache.Folder null) writes neither marker, as before, and the first run happens each launch there; and a window that falls back to software while the platform holds a GPU (a device lost mid-session) writes a CPU marker that the next launch, drawing on the GPU, does not count. (19) REVIEW ROUND 4: A WORK STEP IS BOUNDED. A registered work step (GpuProgram.Work: the voice hardware check, VT-15) was awaited with no limit and no cancellation of its own, so one that never completes (an audio driver that never answers) held the first run, GR-2's Getting ready sheet over the app and FirstRunStartup's one run for ever, cancelled or not, where every draw step is bounded by GpuWarmup.StepTimeout. ENGINEERING DECISION: the work step's await is `working.WaitAsync(StepTimeout, cancellation)`. THE BOUND is GpuWarmup.StepTimeout, 10 s, the same number as a draw step's, for this reason: it is one constant for "a step of the first run that does not answer", the sheet is held by it for at most that long per step, and a hardware check that needs longer than ten seconds on an app's first start is a check the owner would call stuck; a test shortens it for both kinds. WaitAsync ends at the cancellation at once even when the step ignores the token it was handed (the token only asks), so a cancelled run ends promptly as Cancelled. On the timeout the run FAILS (Failed, the message naming the step and the bound) and the step counts as NOT DONE: it is never added to the work done in this process, so no marker of either kind is written for the pass (14) and the next launch prepares again; the run goes on to its end (EndAsync is awaited, the sheet lifts) and the Task it abandoned is observed, so an exception it throws later is not an unobserved task exception. A step that answers after its bound is too late to count. The step itself is not stopped (a Task cannot be): a step that holds a device should honour the cancellation token it is handed. (20) REVIEW ROUND 4: THE CPU MARKER IS KEPT FOR EACH ADAPTER. MarkWarm deleted the whole CPU marker file, so proving one adapter on its GPU took away the prepared state another adapter had (a laptop drawn on its GPU at the desk and on the CPU renderer in a remote desktop session whose adapter DXGI names otherwise: every launch that alternated between them ran the first run again). ENGINEERING DECISION: warm-cpu.txt holds a record of three lines (this build, "cpu", the machine) for each adapter and driver the app was prepared on, as the GPU cache folders are each kept for their adapter (RemoveOthers); WarmedOnCpu reads the record of the machine as it is now; MarkWarmOnCpu writes its own record beside the others (the file written whole, beside then moved; the records of other builds are not read and are dropped when it is written; at most 16 records, the oldest let go); MarkWarm removes only the record of its own machine, and the file when none is left. A record is not removed for an adapter the machine no longer reports: it costs three lines and is read for nothing. A file in the round-3 form (one record) is a file of one record.

## ED-289

[VOICE][ENGINEERING] Voice typing unit VT-1 (Core settings, catalogue, recommender; branch cloud/f-vt-1; the lead numbers it at merge). ENGINEERING DECISIONS where voice-SPEC.md and the OD-0099 picks are silent; none changes an owner ruling. The code is `src/Marrow.Core/Port/Voice/`, the tests `tests/Marrow.Core.Tests/Port/Voice/`.
1. The manifest (V-9.1, V-T1) is C# data, `ModelManifest.cs`, not an embedded resource: `Marrow.Core.csproj` is a protected file and adding an `EmbeddedResource` needs it. The 29 rows were generated from the spec's table by a script; `ModelCatalogTests` re-reads the table from `porting/first-release/voice-SPEC.md` and compares id, bytes, SHA-256, model, version and the English-only column row by row, so a typo in either place fails. The lead may move the rows to a JSON resource when the csproj is next opened.
2. Q-V-14 (ED-267 (4)): `WhisperModel.Note` is null for Medium and Large v3; Tiny, Base and Small keep V-9.1's English-only note and Large v3 Turbo keeps its own ("... it does not translate.").
3. `voiceTyping` JSON (V-16.2, Q-V-19 B, Q-V-1 C): `mic` (the chosen input's device id; null = "Windows default", the first item and the default) and `liveWordsChoice` (`"live"` | `"accurate"`; absent until the slow-PC question is answered) are written only when set, so the default bytes stay V-16.2's `{"engine":"local","lang":null,"model":null}`. Key order: engine, lang, model, mic, liveWordsChoice. Lenient read: an unknown engine is Local, an unknown `lang` string (any code not in the list, or another case) is null, a `model` that is not a catalogue id is null, an empty or non-string `mic` is null, an unknown `liveWordsChoice` is null. The enum `LiveWordsChoice` (Live, Accurate) stands for the two Q-V-1 C answers (live words with a smaller model; the text after you stop with the accurate model).
4. `voiceOrb` JSON (V-16.1): the wire names not spelled in the spec are `"siri"` and `"membrane"` for `orb`; `orbSize` reads only the numbers 32 and 26 (32.0 and 26.0 included), any other value keeps 32. Writer: compact, UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping (a CPU name such as `Intel(R) Core(TM) i5 & ...` is stored as typed, not as \u escapes).
5. `voiceHardware` (V-16.4): `at` is written as `yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ssZ` (UTC, whole seconds) and read with an invariant parse (an unreadable one is the Unix epoch); `vramGB` and `freeVramGB` are numbers (doubles); `FromJson` returns null when nothing readable is stored and otherwise fills missing fields with defaults, the key with "" (so such a record is stale). `HardwareKey` (V-10.5) is SHA-256 over `name:length:text\n` for adapter, driver, cpu, ramGB, app, runtime, written as lower-case hex; the length prefix keeps values that run together from colliding. `IsStale` is an ordinal comparison; no stored result is stale.
6. `VoiceLanguage.Resolve` (V-7.14): a `lang` that is not in the list is treated as null (V-16.2's lenient read, applied again at the call); `ask` resolves to language "auto", named false, ask true; the Windows display language is the part before the first `-` or `_`, lower-cased, kept when it is in the list ("hi-IN" is hi, "fil-PH" and "sw-KE" are auto), so no `CultureInfo` is needed in Core. The reset rule is three functions on the two settings records: `WithLanguageDefault` (stores `langMode`, sets `lang` to null, also when the same default is picked again), `WithQuestionAnswer` (en, hi, ur or auto; anything else throws ArgumentException) and `WithPagePick` (any list code or auto). The Customization page (CZ-7a) and the question (VT-12) call them.
7. `Recommender` (V-10.2): `HardwareProfile` carries VRAM in bytes (3 GB means 3 x 2^30); "a working GPU backend" is `Backend != None`, so a present GPU with no working backend is a processor-only machine; only the code "en" counts as English; the CPU multilingual 8-core row's fallback `medium-q8_0` is the next rung of the ladder (`SelfTestPlan.StepDown`), not a second field; `IsNeverRecommended` is V-10.2's list written out (15 ids).
8. `SelfTestPlan` (V-10.3, Q-V-1 C): a timing at RTF up to 0.15 keeps the model with live words on; above 0.15 up to 0.5 keeps it, leaves live words to the user's answer and asks (`AskUser`); above 0.5 steps down one rung to be timed again, once only. REPLACED by item 13 (lead rulings R1 to R3): the first version kept a model still too slow after the step with live words off and asked nothing, and asked in the middle band with no smaller model to offer.
9. Reason lines (Q-V-4 A, V-10.4): the templates verbatim; `{Model}` is the catalogue name with its English-only mark and without version or size (`Large v3 Turbo`, `Base (English only)`); `t` is RTF x 10 rounded half up to 0.5 s and never below 0.5 (so a measured time is not shown as "0 seconds"); "seconds" is pluralised correctly, "1 second" for exactly one (item 13, lead ruling R4; the first version wrote "1 seconds"); with no measured time for the bigger model the clause after the semicolon is left out and the sentence ends after "seconds".
10. Tests: V-T10 to V-T16 and V-T120 to V-T123 are in `tests/Marrow.Core.Tests/Port/Voice/`, V-T1 and V-T12/V-T13 in `ModelCatalogTests`. Each carries `Trait("Feature","VT-1")`, its `Trait("Spec","V-Txx")` and `Trait("Decision","ED-267")`: R-TEST-1 needs a Req, Rule or Decision trait and ED-267 is the existing Voice typing decision, so it stands in until the lead numbers this entry. `tests/Marrow.Testing/Traceability.cs` was extended (eight lines) so the meta-test accepts the `Feature` and `Spec` traits the first-release units use (formats `VT-1` and `V-T10`); it still demands a Req, Rule or Decision trait on every test. The `SpeechLabel` half of V-T121 (the words with V-6.3's timing) belongs to VT-3, which owns `SpeechLabel`.

12. Review round 1 (unit/integ-vt1, test-first: VoiceCoreReviewTests). `SelfTestPlan.Decide` takes the timing's `RecommendationBasis`: OD-0099 Q-V-1 C's amendment says "a fast PC (every GPU) is never asked and stays live with the accurate model", so a GPU timing at RTF above 0.15 up to 0.5 keeps the model with live words on and asks nothing; what it left to the lead is ruled in item 13.
13. Lead ruling, 2026-10-04, from the OD-0099 Q-V-1 C amendment ("when the speed test finds the PC too slow to run the accurate model live, the app asks the user once ... a fast PC (every GPU) is never asked and stays live with the accurate model"); implemented test-first on unit/integ-vt1 (VoiceCoreReviewTests, VoiceCoreReview2Tests). R1: a timing on a working GPU backend never steps down and never asks, at any RTF; it keeps the model with live words on. The V-10.3 step down applies to the processor basis only. R2: the question is asked only when there is something smaller to offer, a smaller rung on the model's ladder; at the bottom rung (small-q5_1, tiny.en) or on a model on no ladder (large-v3) a slow processor timing keeps the current model with text after the user stops (live words off) and asks nothing. R3 (replaces item 8's second half): the question is asked once whenever a processor timing is too slow for live words (RTF above 0.15) and a smaller rung exists, also after the one step down (the model is kept; there is no second timing); never twice for the same hardware key. "The same hardware key" is settled by R5 below (the first version read it from the stored voiceHardware check, which every check rewrites, so a new key asked or not by the order of its timings, and every app update asked again: the round-3 re-check, VoiceCoreReview3Tests). `Decide(model, rtf, steppedDown, basis, answeredForThisKey)` returns live words null with no question when the answer is already stored for this hardware; R6 then says what it does. R4: the reason lines pluralise correctly ("about 1 second", "about 2 seconds"; 0.5 and 1.5 stay plural); the Q-V-4 A templates are otherwise unchanged. With the rulings, review round 1 also settled (ENGINEERING DECISION, test-first): the settings writers never throw; an enum value outside its wire names is written as the record's default name (an out-of-range `liveWordsChoice` is left out, as no answer), and a NaN or infinite `vramGB`, `freeVramGB` or `rtf` is written as null; both read back as the default (V-16.6). R5 (lead ruling, 2026-10-04, from the OD-0099 Q-V-1 C amendment, "asks the user once ... the answer is kept in Settings > Voice typing and can be changed there"): the answer is stored with the key it was given under, `voiceTyping.liveWordsChoiceKey`, written beside `liveWordsChoice` only when set (the default bytes stay V-16.2's) and read leniently (an empty or non-string value is none). The key is the HARDWARE part of V-10.5's key only, `HardwareKey.ComputeHardwarePart` (SHA-256 over adapter description, driver version, processor name and memory GB, in the same length-prefixed encoding as the full key, under its own leading name), without the app version and build and the Whisper.net runtime version. `SelfTestPlan.AnsweredFor(voiceTyping, today's hardware part)` compares the two and never reads the voiceHardware check; an answer stored without a key (none can be, after R5) counts as not given. The question comes back only when the hardware part changes (a new GPU, driver, processor or memory), never after an app or runtime update; the V-10.5 check itself still re-runs on any key change. R6 (lead ruling, 2026-10-04, from the OD-0099 Q-V-1 C amendment): `SelfTestPlan.ApplyAnswer(model, answer)`: a stored `live` answer takes the next smaller rung on the model's ladder with live words on and is not timed again; `accurate` keeps the model with text after the user stops. ENGINEERING DECISION: `live` on a model with no smaller rung (never asked then, R2) keeps the model with text after the stop, R2's outcome. R7 (lead ruling, 2026-10-04, from the OD-0099 Q-V-1 C amendment): `SelfTestPlan.WithSlowAnswer(voiceTyping, answer, hardware part)` stores the answer with its key; a question dismissed without an answer (null) stores nothing, leaving any earlier answer for other hardware as it was, so the next self-test on the same key asks again. This is the default until the question's design (OD-0070) says otherwise. R8 (lead ruling, 2026-10-04, from the owner's welcome-voice pick in OD-0099, "until answered the accurate model is used"; the round-5 re-check, VoiceCoreReview5Tests, found that a dismissal left no outcome): `SelfTestPlan.ApplyAnswer(model, LiveWordsChoice?)` takes null for a question dismissed or not answered yet and keeps the accurate model with text after the user stops, live words off; the voiceHardware entry's `liveWords` is written from that decision, so false. The answers keep R6's meaning. Round 6 (the re-check of fe05a9f5f, VoiceCoreReview6Tests): `ApplyAnswer` is fed from `SelfTestPlan.AnswerFor(voiceTyping, today's hardware part)`, which gives the stored `liveWordsChoice` only when `AnsweredFor` matches and null otherwise, so an answer kept for other hardware (R7) never decides a dismissed or unanswered question here (R5, R8); never from `liveWordsChoice` directly.

Until it is settled PR-MCP-199 stays open (its STOP is in MCPSettingsPageTestFirstTests) and the measurements above are the comparison to close it with.

DECIDED (built in SwiftFont, see ED-316): the box is keyed by the explicit TEXT STYLE, not the point size, and set as an absolute line height (not natural + 2, not a font-size change; Avalonia centres the extra, baselines 13.7 / 12.9 / 12.0 in Inter, within a point of the Mac's); the implicit default is its own value, SwiftFont.Default. The comparison above now closes: MCPSettingsPageFrameTests draws the lead card 94, the Connected rows 58 / 74 / 58 in a 192 card, the Custom card 97, a catalog card 126 at a 136 pitch and a two-line-title card 144 at a 154 pitch, all equal to the frames; the notice pill at C 9.0 is 33 (TimelineRowsBlitzAbCardTests). (2) THE SCRIPTS EDITOR'S NAME ROW (ED-290-2).
